To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1. the most typical sequences of a family are those which are closest to the centroid of the family; 2. the most representative pairs of sequences are those that maximize the sum of their sequence weights; and 3. the most appropriate number (N) of representative sets of sequences for a family is that for which N+1 sets have the smallest average sequence weight of the Nth set.

(1) a new method for optimal hierarchical clustering of sequences is proposed; (2) the 'core' of homologous families is defined as the subset of sequences with the highest weights; (3) the most representative pair and minimal sets of sequences are identified automatically for each family; (4) the new method is implemented as an online server for structural genomics; (5) the new sequence weight is shown to be more appropriate than the average for the purpose of protein family classification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of methods for the analysis and classification of multiple sequence alignments, which is a key step in the study of protein families.

the development of a new approach for classification of protein families, the selection of the most typical sequences for a given family and a method for automatic identification of a representative subset of sequences from an alignment.
the problem of classifying proteins in general and, in particular, with the problem of identifying representative subsets from multiple alignments of homologous families.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the new methods described in this article can be used to identify the most typical sequences within families of proteins and to select the most informative subsets from multiple alignments.
, while hierarchical classification has been a very useful tool for protein family analysis, it should be complemented by alternative approaches that are more suitable for certain applications.
the new approach is a significant improvement on the traditional one, and that it can be applied to a variety of problems in protein sequence analysis.

the new approach to protein classification is more informative than hierarchical classification and is more suitable for the selection of representative sequences for protein structure determination.
we have developed an approach for protein family classification that is objective, reproducible and, at all levels of granularity, optimal.
we have provided a novel and more objective way to group related proteins and have developed a new method to select the most appropriate representatives from a set of aligned sequences.

it is not possible to classify proteins in a meaningful way without taking into consideration the distribution of sequence similarity along the length of an alignment.
